Available online at www.sciencedirect.com
Precambrian Research 163 (2008) 239–264
Paleomagnetism of Proterozoic maﬁc dikes from the
Tobacco Root Mountains, southwest Montana
Stephen S. Harlan a,∗, John Wm. Geissman b, Lawrence W. Sneec
a Department of Environmental Science and Policy, George Mason University, 4400 University Drive, MS 5F2, Fairfax, VA 22030-4444, United States
b Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, MSC03 2040 University of New Mexico, Albuquerque, NM 87131, United States
c U.S. Geological Survey, P .O. Box 25046, MS 980 Federal Center , Denver , CO 80225, United States
Received 11 September 2007; received in revised form 16 December 2007; accepted 23 December 2007
Abstract
Paleomagnetic data from Proterozoic maﬁc dikes in southwestern Montana provides evidence for two distinct episodes of subparallel dike
emplacement at ca. 1450 and 780 Ma. Published geochemical data from dikes in the southern Tobacco Root Mountains has identiﬁed three distinct
compositional groups, termed groups A, B, and C. Geochronological data from the group A dikes yielded a Sm–Nd age of 1448± 49 Ma. Emplace-
ment of these dikes is thought to reﬂect maﬁc magmatism associated with extension accompanying development of the adjacent Mesoproterozoic
Belt Basin. Paleomagnetic results from these dikes and a group C dike yield antipodal magnetizations with a group-mean direction of D = 225.0
◦,
I = 61.8◦ (k = 27.9, α95 = 7.7◦, N = 14 independent means/24 sites). The average paleomagnetic pole (8.7◦N, 216.1◦E, A95 = 10.3◦) is considered to
be primary on the basis of positive baked contact tests and similarity to poles of ca. 1.45–1.4 Ga from intrusions elsewhere in North America, but is
discordant with respect to poles from age equivalent sedimentary rocks of the Meosoproterozoic Belt Supergroup.
40Ar/39Ar dates from geochemical
group B dikes are consistent with published U–Pb dates that demonstrate dike emplacement at 780 Ma as part of the regional Gunbarrel magmatic
event. Hornblende concentrates from the group B dikes yield
40Ar/39Ar apparent ages of 778–772 Ma, whereas biotite from a baked contact zone
yielded a plateau date of 788 Ma. Paleomagnetic results from the group B dikes yield a mean direction ofD = 301.5◦, I = −17.1◦ (k = 65.7,α95 = 4.0◦,
N = 12 independent means/23 sites) with a paleomagnetic pole at 14.6 ◦N, 127.0◦E( A95 = 3.2◦). The combination of geochronologic data, results
of a baked contact test, and spatial agreement of the paleomagnetic poles with poles of similar age elsewhere in North America indicates that
this is also a primary magnetization associated with dike emplacement. Paleomagnetic data from some of the Tobacco Root Mountains dikes
provide evidence that they were partially to completely remagnetized during latest Cretaceous to early Tertiary time, perhaps due to thermal affects
associated with emplacement of the Late Cretaceous Tobacco Root Batholith. The overall agreement of paleomagnetic poles from the Proterozoic
dikes with those of age equivalent rocks elsewhere in North America and agreement of the secondary magnetization with expected directions for
the latest Cretaceous/early Tertiary indicate that the rocks of the Tobacco Root Mountains have not experienced signiﬁcant tilting or vertical axis
rotation since the Mesoproterozoic. The new paleomagnetic poles from this study thus provide key data for reﬁning Meso- and Neoproterozoic
parts of the North American APW path.

Keywords: Paleomagnetism; Geochronology; Dike emplacement; Apparent polar wander; Proterozoic; Tectonics
1. Introduction
Proterozoic maﬁc dikes are a common feature of several
Laramide-age (latest Cretceous–early Tertiary) basement-cored
uplifts of southwestern Montana ( Fig. 1A and B). Most dikes
strike west or northwest and cut Archean crystalline base-
ment. Many dikes parallel or are subparallel to basement
∗ Corresponding author. Tel.: +1 703 993 3892; fax: +1 703 993 1066.
E-mail address: sharlan@gmu.edu (S.S. Harlan).
faults of presumed Precambrian ancestry. Dike emplacement
and faults are thought to have accompanied extension that
formed the adjacent Mesoproterozoic Belt Basin ( Harrison et
al., 1974; Wooden et al., 1978; Schmidt and Garihan, 1986;
Harlan et al., 2005 ). Based on geochemical data from dikes
in the Ruby Range and southern Tobacco Root Mountains,
Wooden et al. (1978) identiﬁed three distinct geochemical
groups, with apparent ages of ca. 1450 Ma and 1120–1130 Ma.
These ages are similar to dates from maﬁc sills that intrude sed-
imentary rocks of the Belt Supergroup ( Hunt, 1962; Zartman
et al., 1982; H ¨oy, 1989; Anderson and Davis, 1995; Sears

et al., 1998 ) and to metamorphic dates from those strata

distinct episodes of tectonism and/or sedimentation within
the Belt Basin; however, recent high-precision geochronol-
ogy has demonstrated that most of the Belt Supergroup
was deposited between 1470 and 1400 Ma ( Evans et al.,

### page_3
S.S. Harlan et al. / Precambrian Research 163 (2008) 239–264 241
We report new paleomagnetic results from Proterozoic maﬁc
dikes exposed in the Tobacco Root Mountains of southwest
Montana. Our goal in undertaking this study was to better
understand the age, distribution, and tectonic importance of Pro-
terozoic maﬁc dikes emplaced along the northwest margin of the
Wyoming craton, and to contribute temporally well-constrained
paleomagnetic poles to the North American apparent polar wan-
der (APW) path. Because the ca. 1.4 and 1.1 Ga segments of
the North American APW path are relatively well deﬁned, and
assuming that post-emplacement deformation has been minimal,
these data could be used to conﬁrm whether multiple episodes
of dike intrusion occurred in southwest Montana. If primary
magnetizations could not be isolated because of subsequent
remagnetization(s), the paleomagnetic data could help resolve
the age and nature of post-emplacement events affecting the dike
isotopic systems. Our paleomagnetic data yield three distinct
magnetizations. Two of these are primary, having been acquired
during dike emplacement during Proterozoic time, whereas the
third is a product of latest Cretaceous remagnetization. Compar-
ison of the primary dike paleomagnetic poles with those from
Proterozoic rocks elsewhere in North America indicates that
dikes of two ofWooden et al.’s (1978)geochemical groups were
emplaced at ca. 1450 Ma, with a third distinct group emplaced
at 780 Ma. The paleomagnetic and
40Ar/39Ar data reported here
are consistent with Sm–Nd and U–Pb results from the southern
Tobacco Root dikes, which provided evidence for dike intru-
sion at 1448 and 780 Ma (Harlan et al., 2005). New
40Ar/39Ar
dates from hornblende from maﬁc dikes and a biotite from a
contact gneiss sample reported here provide further evidence in
support of Neoproterozoic magmatism in the southern Tobacco
Root Mountains. The ca. 1448 Ma dikes are related to extension
in the Belt Basin, whereas the younger group B dikes are part of
a regional magmatic episode termed the Gunbarrel maﬁc mag-
matic event that extended from northwestern Wyoming to the
Arctic Ocean and was a precursor to Neoproterozoic breakup
of the Rodinian supercontinent ( Harlan et al., 2003b ). Paleo-
magnetic poles from this event are key reference poles that may
be used to assess the validity of competing continental recon-
structions for Rodinia (Park et al., 1995b; Harlan et al., 2003b;
Bleeker, 2004). Although summary poles utilizing paleomag-
netic data from the Gunbarrel dikes have been cited by numerous
authors, the details of paleomagnetic results from the southern
Tobacco Root dikes have not been published.
2. Geological setting
The Tobacco Root Mountains are a broadly domal, basement-
cored uplift located at the intersection of two Laramide (Late
Cretaceous–early Tertiary) tectonic provinces: (1) the Rocky
Mountain foreland, characterized by basement-involved defor-
mation along low- to moderate-angle reverse faults; and (2)
thin-skinned thrusts and folds of the Helena salient of the
Cordilleran thrust belt, within which deformation is limited
largely to sedimentary strata of Mesoproterozoic to Mesozoic
age ( Fig. 1 B). Superimposed on structures of both tectonic
provinces are normal faults developed during late Cenozoic
to Recent extension that produced the present-day basins and
ranges of southwestern Montana (Reynolds, 1979; Schmidt and
Garihan, 1986; Kellogg et al., 1995).
The Tobacco Root Mountains expose one of the northern-
most parts of Archean crystalline basement in the Wyoming
craton (Fig. 1A). The basement rocks are comprised of rocks
of the Montana Metasedimentary Province, a terrane charac-
terized by metasedimentary rocks, including marble, quartizite,
iron formation, and pelitic schist ( Mogk et al., 1992, 2004 ).
In the Tobacco Root Mountains, the basement rocks are domi-
nated by three distinct lithologic assemblages ( Vitaliano et al.,
1979; Mogk et al., 2004; Burger et al., 2004 ): (1) the Indian
Creek Metamorphic Suite; (2) the Pony-Middle Mountain Meta-
morphic Suite; and (3) the Sphuler Peak Metamorphic Suite.
The Indian Creek and Pony-Middle Mountain suites are dom-
inated by quartzofeldspathic gneiss and variable amounts of
metamorphosed supracrustal rocks. The Sphuler Peak Metamor-
phic Suite is dominated by amphibolite, with lesser amounts of
quartzite and aluminous schist. The Indian Creek and Pony-
Middle Mountain metamorphic suites are interpreted to be part
of a platform-type sedimentary sequence deposited on a late
Archean continental margin ( Mogk and Henry, 1988; Wooden
et al., 1988; Mogk et al., 2004), whereas the Sphuler Peak Meta-
morphic Suite is thought to have originated as oceanic crust
(Burger et al., 2004). Gneisses from the central part of the range
have protolith crystallization ages of 3.2–3.4 Ga and record evi-
dence for metamorphism at ca. 2.8 Ga ( Mueller et al., 2004 ).
Pb–Pb monozite and zircon age determinations from record evi-
dence of high-grade metamorphism and/or magmatism at ca.
2.4 Ga, but no rocks of this age have been identiﬁed in the
Tobacco Root Mountains (Cheney et al., 2004a; Mueller et al.,
2004). Rocks of the Indian Peak and Pony-Middle Mountain
metamorphic suites are cut by amphibolite dikes and sills termed
Proterozoic Metamorphic Maﬁc Dikes and Sills ( Brady et al.,
2004b); one of these intrusions yielded a U–Pb zircon crys-
tallization age of 2.060 ± 0.006 Ga (Mueller et al., 2004 ). The
amphibolites are interpreted to represent tholeittic dikes and sills
intruded into cool crust, perhaps associated with continental rift-
ing of the Wyoming craton ( Brady et al., 2004a ). The 2.06 Ga
age for these dikes is similar to several ca. 2.1–2.0 Ga U–Pb dates
reported from NE-striking dikes along the south and southeast-
ern margins of the Wyoming craton that have also been attributed
to continental extension, rifting, and development of a passive
continental margin at ca. 2.2–2.1 Ga. It has been hypothesized
that this extensional event records break up and dismember-
ment of the Wyoming and Superior cratons at this time prior
to their reassembly at ca. 1.8 Ga (Karlstrom et al., 1981; Premo
and Van Schmus, 1989; Cox et al., 2000; Roscoe and Card,
1993; Chamberlain et al., 2003; Harlan et al., 2003a; Bowers
and Chamberlain, 2006; Duebendorfer et al., 2006).
Rocks of the Indian Creek Metamorphic Suite, the Pony-
Middle Mountain Metamorphic Suite, the Sphuler Peak
Metamorphic Suite and the maﬁc rocks of the Proterozoic Meta-
morphic Maﬁc Dikes and Sills were tectonically juxtaposed and
regionally metamorphosed to at least upper amphibolite facies,
at ca. 1.77 Ga, during a widespread tectonothermal event that
some workers have termed the “Big Sky Orogeny” ( Brady et
al., 2004a,b; Cheney et al., 2004a,b; Harms et al., 2004 ). This

### page_4
242 S.S. Harlan et al. / Precambrian Research 163 (2008) 239–264
deformational event is thought to represent deep burial dur-
ing a continental-scale collision, perhaps due to collision of
the Hearne Province or other terrane to the north and west
with the Wyoming craton. Collision may have been followed
by isothermal decompression, probably due to rapid tectonic
denudation late in the orogenic cycle ( Cheney et al., 2004a ),
as suggested by mineral dates from rocks in southwest Montana
from several geochronologic systems. U–Pb zircon,
207Pb/206Pb
monazite, K–Ar, and40Ar/39Ar yield similar apparent ages rang-
ing from 1.82 to 1.70 Ga (Giletti, 1966, 1971; Erslev and Sutter,
1990; Vargo, 1990; Harlan et al., 1996; Roberts et al., 2002;
Brady et al., 2004a; Cheney et al., 2004b; Mueller et al., 2004).
Alternatively, Mueller et al. (2004) propose that the 1.77 Ga
tectonothermal event may be related to post-collision maﬁc
underplating, extension, and rapid exhumation of the entire
region.
The Archean basement rocks in the Tobacco Root Moun-
tains are cut by unmetamorphosed Proterozoic diabase dikes that
strike N70
◦W, are near vertical, and cut the northeast-striking
metamorphic foliation of the basement rocks ( Koehler, 1973;
Vitaliano et al., 1979)( Fig. 2A). Individual dikes range from 0.3
to 110 m in thickness, and are up to 10-km long. Although many
dikes are shown as continuous features in geologic mapping
by Vitaliano et al. (1979) (Fig. 2 A), our observations indi-
cate that many are discontinuous. In the northern Tobacco Root
Mountains, the dikes strike N30
◦Wt oN 5 0◦W and are exposed
subparallel to, or along, northwest-striking Laramide reverse
faults and occupy the axial regions of several foreland anticlines
(Fig. 2B). One of these, the Mammoth dike, is 250–300 m thick
and is locally highly differentiated (Koehler, 1973).
The Precambrian rocks of the Tobacco Root Mountains
were overlain by sedimentary rocks during the Paleozoic and
Mesozoic, but these rocks were stripped from the range during
Laramide deformation and now crop out only in the northern and
northwestern parts of the range. The core of the range consists
of the granodioritic Tobacco Root Batholith of Late Cretaceous
age, which has yielded K–Ar dates of 77–72 Ma ( Vitaliano et
al., 1980). Numerous Late Cretaceous or early Tertiary satellitic
sills, dikes, and plugs are also present in the northern and south-
ern Tobacco Root Mountains. Eocene and Oligocene volcanic
rocks form a broad volcanic plateau north of Virginia City, in
the southeast Tobacco Root Mountains (Fig. 2A).
The west- and northwest-striking dikes of southwestern Mon-
tana are a pervasive tectonic element of these basement-cored
uplifts and their origin and tectonic importance has long been
the subject of speculation. Based on Rb–Sr dates, the dikes were
considered to reﬂect maﬁc magmatism accompanying develop-
ment of the nearby Mesoproterozoic Belt Basin (Wooden et al.,
1978; Schmidt and Hendrix, 1981; Schmidt and Garihan, 1986).
The dikes are found in, or parallel to subparallel to, faults inter-
preted to have been reactivated as basement-involved reverse or
thrust structures in the latest Cretaceous. Schmidt and Garihan
(1986) proposed that the dikes were intruded parallel to or along
normal faults formed during northeast- and southwest-directed
basement extension accompanying development of the Helena
Embayment of the Mesoproterozoic Belt Basin, exposed to the
west and northwest. Many of the Mesoproterozoic normal faults
were reactivated during Laramide shortening as reverse faults
and/or as normal faults during late Cenozoic extension. The
Rb–Sr dates of 1450 and 1130 Ma were interpreted to record dis-
tinct episodes of tectonism and sedimentation in the Belt Basin
and both dates are similar to isotopic dates reported from maﬁc
sills and sedimentary rocks elsewhere in the basin ( Wooden et
al., 1978).
In the southern Tobacco Root Mountains, Wooden et al.
(1978) identiﬁed three groups of dikes based on major and
trace element geochemistry, which they termed A, B, and C.
Group A dikes are fresh to somewhat altered and are ﬁne-
to medium-grained ( ≤1 to 2 mm average grain size) diabase.
They consist of clinopyroxene (augite) and plagioclase, with
minor biotite and amphibole. Maﬁc minerals are slightly altered
to chlorite, and plagioclase is saussuritized. These dikes are
ophitic and subophitic to intergranular; porphyritic and glom-
eroporphyritic textures are sometimes present. Group A dikes
are thin, with thicknesses ranging from 2 to 7 m. The dikes are
chemically undifferentiated, display moderate iron-enrichment,
and are among the most primitive of the dikes in the southern
Tobacco Root Mountains (Wooden et al., 1978). The southern
Tobacco Root dikes are petrographically and chemically similar
to dikes from the nearby Ruby Range to the southwest, and rep-
resent a common magma emplaced at the same time ( Wooden
et al., 1978).
Group B dikes are composed of clinopyroxene (augite) and
plagioclase, but also contain hornblende and biotite. A striking
feature of these dikes is the presence of graphic intergrowths
of quartz, plagioclase, and alkali-feldspar. Magnetite, ilmenite,
sulﬁde minerals (chalcopyrite), and apatite are common acces-
sory phases. Group B dikes are commonly altered: plagioclase
is replaced by clay minerals and white mica, and hornblende,
biotite, and pyroxene are altered to chlorite and blue-green
ﬁbrous amphibole. This alteration is deuteric in origin, and
occurred during protracted cooling and hydrothermal circulation
following emplacement. The dikes have well-deﬁned chilled
margins and have medium- to coarse-grained (2–5 mm) inte-
riors where they exhibit ophitic to gabbroic textures. In the
southern Tobacco Root Mountains, their coarse grain size, abun-
dance of hydrous minerals, graphic intergrowths, and thickness
(10–110 m) distinguish them from either group A or C dikes.
The group B dikes are iron-enriched and are quartz normative
(Wooden et al., 1978).
Group C dikes are represented by samples from only two
dikes (Wooden et al., 1978 ). These dikes are ﬁne to medium
grained, have intergranular textures, and consist of clinopyrox-
ene (augite–pigeonite) and plagioclase, with minor hornblende,
biotite, and oxides. Plagioclase is moderately altered and some
pyroxenes are mantled by secondary amphibole or chlorite.
Group C dikes are characterized by low iron and moderately
high alkali and silica contents (Wooden et al., 1978).
Rb–Sr results from group A dikes in the southern Tobacco
Root Mountains gave a limited spread of Rb–Sr ratios and were
not amenable to an age calculation (Wooden, 1975). Rb–Sr ratios
from similar dikes in the Ruby Range, have a greater spread in
87Rb/86Sr versus 87Sr/86Sr ratios, providing an isochron age of
1455 ± 125 Ma with an initial87Sr/86Sr ratio of 0.7019± 0.0008

(Wooden et al., 1978). Most Rb–Sr data from the Tobacco Root
group A dikes scatter about this isochron. Wooden et al. (1978)
argued that the age obtained from the Ruby Range dikes best
represents the age of emplacement of the group A dikes in
the southern Tobacco Root Mountains. Group B Rb–Sr data
are scattered; hence, their geochronologic interpretation is more
complicated than the group A dikes. Data from three localities
appear to deﬁne a linear array that Wooden et al. (1978)used to
calculate an age of 1120± 185 Ma, with an initial
87Sr/86Sr ratio
of 0.7025± 0.0022. Other, more highly altered samples formed
parallel isochrons with higher initial ratios. The petrographi-
cally freshest group C samples gave an apparent Rb–Sr age of
1130 ± 130 Ma, with an87Sr/86Sr initial ratio of 0.709± 0.002.
Although this age is statistically indistinguishable from that of
the group B dikes, their compositions and initial ratios indicate
that they are not comagmatic (Wooden et al., 1978).
Recent geochronologic work by Harlan et al. (2005) reﬁned
the emplacement history of the Tobacco Root Dikes. Sm–Nd
mineral dating of a group A dike yielded an apparent age of
1448 ± 49 Ma, which is considered to be the best estimate of
the age of emplacement of these dikes. Because group A and
group C dikes yield similar remanent magnetizations (as we

### page_6
244 S.S. Harlan et al. / Precambrian Research 163 (2008) 239–264
report below), Harlan et al. (2005) suggested that dikes of both
geochemical groups were emplaced at about the same time, and
this age is in good agreement with U–Pb dates from sills in
Belt Supergroup strata exposed to the north and west of the
Tobacco Root Mountains ( Zartman et al., 1982; H ¨oy, 1989;
Hunt, 1962; Anderson and Davis, 1995; Sears et al., 1998) and
from dikes exposed in the basement of foreland uplifts else-
where in Wyoming (Chamberlain and Frost, 1995). U–Pb dating
of zircon and baddeleyite from the more differentiated group
B dikes yielded an apparent age of 787 ± 11 Ma, although the
zircons used in the analysis were discordant. An identical, but
analytically more precise, upper intercept age of 782.4± 4.9 Ma
was determined using four baddeleyite analyses. Because bad-
deleyite is a primary igneous phase in maﬁc dikes and thus is
unaffected by inheritance, the upper intercept age was consid-
ered to represent the best estimate of the age of emplacement of
the group B dikes (Harlan et al., 2005).
To supplement the geochronological date reported byHarlan
et al. (2005) , we report additional data consistent with the
Neoproterozoic age for the group B dikes described above.
These provide evidence for a lack of signiﬁcant tectonother-
mal disturbance of the dike and basement rocks in the southern
Tobacco Root Mountains. Unfortunately, samples appropriate
for
40Ar/39Ar dating could not be obtained from any Group
A dikes. 40Ar/39Ar dates from hornblende from the group B
dikes and biotite from basement gneiss in the thermal contact
zone of a 100-m thick group B dike yield additional Neopro-
terozoic age estimates ( Fig. 3 ). Analytical data and methods
are presented in Table 1. Four hornblende concentrates from
hand samples from paleomagnetic sites in three group B dikes
(TR6, TR19, TR21, and TR62) yield similar apparent age spec-
tra (Fig. 3A and B). The age spectra are complicated, yielding
somewhat U-shaped spectra some excess
40Ar in high- and
low-temperature steps, but which also yield relatively ﬂat and
consistent ages for intermediate temperature steps (Table 1). Two
of these samples yield identical plateau dates of 775 ± 5M a
(2σ). The other two fail to satisfy the strict plateau crite-
ria of Fleck et al. (1977) , but give weighted mean apparent
ages of 778 ± 3 and 772 ± 5 Ma for the intermediate temper-
ature steps. We consider both the plateau and weighted mean
dates to represent reasonable estimates for the emplacement
age of these dikes. These dates are consistent with the U–Pb
baddeleyite data from the dikes, especially considering incor-
poration of decay constant errors for both isotopic systems.
Biotite obtained from the contact zone of paleomagnetic site
TR50 (Fig. 3C), described below, also yields a plateau date of
787 ± 4 Ma, and suggests that the
40Ar/39Ar system of the adja-
cent basement rocks was almost completely reset by intrusion of
the dike, although incorporation of excess
40Ar during cooling
may explain why it gives an apparent age somewhat older than
the corresponding dikes. Elsewhere in the Tobacco Root Moun-
tains, hornblende and biotite
40Ar/39Ar dates of 1.7 Ga (Brady
et al., 2004a ) have been reported from basement rocks indi-
cating that they have not been thermally disturbed by younger
tectonothermal processes, with the possible exception of rocks
adjacent to Late Cretaceous intrusions, since cooling through
hornblende and biotite closure temperatures (500 and 300
◦C,

3. Paleomagnetic sampling and analysis
Paleomagnetic samples were collected from 46 sites in dikes
from the southern Tobacco Root Mountains (Fig. 2A), and from
three sites in the northern part of the range ( Fig. 2 B). Our
sites are concentrated in the southwest corner of the range,
where excellent dike exposures are found in several drainages

Note: 40Ar/39Ara is measured atmospheric argon used for mass-discrimination at the time of analysis; 40ArR is radiogenic 40Ar in volts signal; 39ArK is potassium-
derived 39Ar in volts signal; 40ArR/39ArK is the ratio of 40ArR to39ArK after correction for mass-discrimination and interfering isotopes; 39Ar/37Ar = ratio of39ArK
to 37ArCa (this value can be converted to the approximate K/Ca by multiplying by 0.5); %40ArK and %39Ar are the percent of radiogenic 40Ar and percent of total
39Ar released in each temperature step. Temperature steps in italics are those used in the calculation of the plateau or weighted-mean age. Conversion of volts signal
to moles Ar can be made using a conversion factor of 2.078 × 10−12 moles argon per volt of signal. The hornblendes and biotite used in this study were crushed,
sieved, and mineral separates concentrated using standard density (heavy liquid), and magnetic techniques. Biotite sample TR50 was obtained from paleomagnetic
drill core samples used in a baked contact test and were collected within 20 cm of the dike contact. The samples were subjected to AF demagnetization pri or to
preparation of the mineral separations. Optically pure (>99.9%) mineral separates were produced by hand-picking. Mineral separates and neutron ﬂux monitors were
wrapped in aluminum foil packages, placed in quartz vials, and irradiated in the U.S. Geological Survey TRIGA reactor. Variations in neutron ﬂux were monitored
by placing 6–10 standards along the length of each vial; the geometry of the package was such that each sample was adjacent to at least one standard. The ﬂ ux
monitor used in this study was MMhb-1, which has an assigned K–Ar age of 523.1± 2.6 Ma (Renne et al., 1998). Corrections for interfering isotopes were made by
measuring the argon isotopes of K2SO4 and CaF2 irradiated in each package. Each sample was heated in a double-vacuum resistance furnace for 20 min in a series
of 10–20 steps to a maximum temperature of 1450 ◦C. Five isotopes of argon ( 40Ar, 39Ar, 38Ar, 37Ar, and 36Ar) were measured at each temperature step using a
Mass Analyzer Products (MAP 215) mass spectrometer at the U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, operated in the static mode, and the isotopic compositions were
corrected for mass discrimination. Apparent ages were calculated using the decay constants ofSteiger and J¨ager (1977). The determination of whether apparent ages
in individual age spectra constituted a plateau was made using the criteria of Fleck et al. (1977) . Following these criteria, a plateau is deﬁned as comprising two
or more contiguous gas fractions that yield apparent ages that are statistically identical at 95% conﬁdence (using the critical value test of Dalrymple and Lanphere
(1969)) and which together constitute greater than 50% of the total potassium-derived 39ArK released in the step-heating experiment. Individual mean ages were
calculated using a weighted mean, where weighting is by the inverse of the analytical variance. Calculation of the total gas and plateau dates includes the analytical
uncertainty in the determination of the ﬂux parameter J.
(Fig. 2A). Sampling was conducted in order to asses the pos-
sibility of paleomagnetic differences between the geochemical
groups identiﬁed byWooden et al. (1978)and in order to evaluate
the validity of the isotopic dates identiﬁed by the original Rb–Sr
determinations. Most dikes were sampled at more than one site
in order to minimize effects of possible lightning strikes, alter-
ation, or variation in magnetic properties on the natural remanent
magnetization (NRM) of the samples. Basement rocks adjacent
to dikes were sampled at four sites to provide data for baked
contact tests (Everitt and Clegg, 1962) to determine if the dike
magnetizations are primary or secondary. For comparison pur-
poses, samples from three sites were collected from basement
rocks well-removed from the thermal effects of the dikes, and
one site was collected from a small Late Cretaceous intrusion.
Between 7 and 16 samples were obtained at each site using
a portable drill, with each sample oriented using magnetic
and solar compasses and a clinometer. The natural rema-
nent magnetization (NRM) of each specimen was measured
using cryogenic or spinner magnetometers. Detailed progressive
alternating ﬁeld (AF) and/or thermal demagnetization was con-
ducted on all samples. Demagnetization results were assessed
using orthogonal vector diagrams, stereographic projections,

### page_9
S.S. Harlan et al. / Precambrian Research 163 (2008) 239–264 247
and normalized magnetic intensity decay plots. Characteris-
tic and secondary components of magnetization, recognized
by co-linear demagnetization paths on vector diagrams, were
calculated using principal components analysis ( Kirschvink,
1980). Where demagnetization failed to isolate a single char-
acteristic direction or stable endpoint but yielded a curvilinear
demagnetization trajectory due to overlapping coercivity and/or
unblocking temperatures, we calculated remagnetization cir-
cles ( McFadden and McElhinny, 1988 ). Site mean directions
from sites consisting solely of well-deﬁned linear data were
calculated using standard Fisher (1953) statistics; site mean
directions based on a combination of linear and great circle
data were calculated using the maximum likelihood approach
method of McFadden and McElhinny (1988) . Magnetic carri-
ers were identiﬁed by demagnetization characteristics during
AF or thermal demagnetization, acquisition and AF demagne-
tization of both isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) and
anhysteretic remanent magnetization (ARM) experiments, and
by Curie temperature determinations. Curie temperature deter-
minations were made in air in saturating ﬁelds of 0.2–0.4 T
using an electrobalance similar to that described by Larson et
al. (1975) . Additionally, low-frequency magnetic susceptibil-
ity versus temperature determinations were made in a ﬂowing
argon atmosphere using a Kappabridge similar to that described
by Hrouda (1995). Petrographic examination of Fe-oxide phases
in reﬂected light using an oil immersion lens was also used to
investigate the carriers of magnetization in some dike samples.
4. Paleomagnetic results and interpretation
Ninety-three percent of the Tobacco Root dike samples gave
interpretable results after AF or thermal demagnetization, and
three distinct magnetizations were identiﬁed. Two of these mag-
netizations correspond to dikes represented by geochemical
groups A and B, identiﬁed by Wooden et al. (1978); however,
to distinguish the magnetization groups from the geochem-
ical groups, we term these the A
1 and B 1 magnetizations.
As discussed below, we consider these to be primary ther-
moremanent magnetizations (TRMs) that record two distinct
episodes of dike emplacement during the Proterozoic. An addi-
tional magnetization, termed the R magnetization, is probably
a Late Cretaceous or early Tertiary secondary remanence that
completely overprinted primary dike magnetizations at some
localities. The small percentage of samples that did not yield
interpretable results are characterized by erratic directional
behavior or intensity changes during demagnetization, or were
dominated by low coercivity magnetizations of inconsistent ori-
entation. Because many of these samples had NRM intensities
greater than 15 A/m, we suspect that they have been struck
by lightning. Data from these samples will not be considered
further.
4.1. A
1 Magnetization
Samples from 24 sites in the southern Tobacco Root Moun-
tains and one site in the northern Tobacco Root Mountains give
characteristic remanent magnetizations (ChRM) of south and
southwest declination (D) and moderate to steep positive incli-
nation ( I) or north and northeast declination and moderate to
steep negative inclination. For the purposes of this discussion,
we refer to these as normal and reverse polarity magnetiza-
tions but note that these terms refer to present-day coordinates
only and make no inference regarding the hemisphere in
which the magnetization was acquired. This magnetization is
found in dikes that belong to geochemical groups A and C
of Wooden et al. (1978) , and in some previously unmapped
dikes in both the northern and southern Tobacco Root Moun-
tains.
Fig. 4. In situ orthogonal vector diagrams and equal-area projections showing the behavior of paleomagnetic samples from group A dikes during therma l and
AF demagnetization. Demagnetization results from individual sites from group A dikes show discrete antipodal magnetizations that are well deﬁned d uring the
demagnetization experiments; this magnetization is termed the A1 remanence. For the equal area projections, solid symbols are projections on the lower hemisphere
and open circles are projections on the upper hemisphere. For the vector diagrams, solid circles are projections onto the horizontal plane, and open circles represent
projections on the vertical plane.

NRM directions from these samples are scattered, but largely
deﬁne a plane that contains both normal and reverse polar-
ity magnetizations and the direction of the present day ﬁeld
(i.e. D =1 3
◦, I =7 0◦). NRM intensities range from 18.6× 10−3
to 19.9 × 101 A/m, with a geometric mean of 1.76 A/m. Most
samples contained two magnetic components. The ﬁrst magne-
tization removed is usually of north declination and moderate
positive inclination; a mode calculated from the overprint direc-
tions is D = 1.3
◦, I = 75.8◦ (β95 = 9.4◦), which is essentially
identical to the direction of the present-day ﬁeld. This rema-
nence is usually removed by AF demagnetization of 5–20 mT
or by temperatures less than 350
◦C. The direction and demag-
netization characteristics indicate that this is probably a viscous
remanent magnetization (VRM) acquired in the present-day
ﬁeld. Other low coercivity/low laboratory unblocking temper-
ature overprints are inconsistent in orientation and their origin
is unclear; an exception is discussed below.
Following removal of secondary magnetizations, 72% of the
samples from this group showed behavior in which the paleo-
magnetic vector decayed linearly to the origin of their vector
diagram during AF or thermal demagnetization (Fig. 4B). Such
behavior usually indicates the isolation of a single demagneti-
zation component, which we consider to be the sample ChRM
(“stable endpoint”). Directions for the stable endpoints were
well deﬁned by principal components analysis (PCA), as indi-
cated by maximum angular deviation (MAD) values of 2
◦ to
11◦, with 91% ≤7◦. The stable endpoints deﬁne two approx-
imately antipodal clusters. Four percent of the samples failed
to yield stable endpoints, but gave curvilinear demagnetization
paths that converged toward either the normal or reverse polarity
A
1 direction during demagnetization. This behavior is caused by
the presence of two magnetizations of similar coercivity and/or
laboratory unblocking temperature spectra such that a stable
endpoint could not be isolated. For these samples, magnetiza-

Site-mean directions are generally well grouped as evidenced
by Fisher (1953)k values that ranged from 17 to 244 andα95 val-
ues of 3.6–16.2◦ (Table 2; Fig. 5A). Where multiple sites were
collected from the same dike, the dike mean direction was cal-
culated by averaging site-mean directions (three or more sites)
or by averaging sample directions (only two sites). This gave
what we interpret to be 14 independent recordings of the geo-
magnetic ﬁeld ( Fig. 5B). The reverse and normal group-mean
directions (D = 248.7
◦, I = 63.5◦, k = 71.6,α95 = 8.0◦, N = 6 dike

means, and D = 30.0◦, I = -58.2◦, k = 33.8,α95 = 9.7◦, N = 8 dike
means) (Table 3), after inversion to a common normal polarity,
have an angular difference of 18.4 ± 8.8◦ using the method of
Debiche and Watson (1995). The similarity in directions indi-
cates that remanence acquisition must have spanned at least two
polarity chrons, but overall the data do not yield a positive rever-
sal test using the criteria of McFadden and McElhinny (1990)
(i.e. γ
o = 19.3◦; γc = 12.4◦). Combining the normal and reverse
polarity site-mean directions yields a grand-mean direction of
D = 45.0
◦, I = −61.8◦ (k = 27.9, α95 = 7.5◦, N = 14) ( Fig. 5 B;
Table 2).
Paleomagnetic and rock magnetic evidence indicates that
the A 1 remanence is carried by magnetite. In general, the
reverse polarity A 1 samples are characterized by low to
moderate (10–30 mT) median destructive ﬁelds (MDFs) and
distributed to discrete laboratory unblocking temperatures.
Complete unblocking occurred at temperatures below 580
◦C,
the Curie temperature of pure magnetite. Normalized inten-
sity curves show an initial exponential decay of the magnetic
moment during AF demagnetization ( Fig. 6 A), followed by
gradual decay at higher ﬁelds. Saturation of IRM occurs in ﬁelds
less than 200 mT indicating that the remanence is dominated by
a low coercivity phase. The ChRM of these samples is proba-
bly carried by a combination of multidomain and single domain
magnetite (Fig. 6B). In contrast, normal polarity samples usually
have greater MDFs (i.e. 30–60 mT), have less well deﬁned sec-
ondary magnetizations, and thermally discrete or “knee-shaped”
laboratory unblocking temperatures less than 580
◦C. These
samples are commonly more altered than samples that contain
the reverse polarity ChRM. Their normalized AF decay curves
are of single-domain form (Dunlop and ¨Ozdemir, 1997). Strong-
ﬁeld thermomagnetic determinations from normal and reverse
polarity samples are essentially identical and give reversible
heating and cooling curves (Fig. 6C) with a single Curie temper-
ature at 568 ± 8
◦C (1S.D.; n = 5 samples). The paleomagnetic
and rock magnetic characteristics of these samples indicate that
low-Ti titanomagnetite carries the A
1 magnetization in these
rocks.
Two baked contact tests were conducted on dikes with the
A1 magnetization in order to determine whether the A 1 mag-
netization is a primary thermoremanent magnetization (TRM)
or a secondary magnetization acquired at some later time. The
ﬁrst test is from samples collected within 0.3 m of an 8-m wide
dike that has a ChRM of D = 14.6
◦ and I = −62.3◦ (k = 54.4,
α95 = 16.9◦, N = 3 sites; dike 2,Table 2). The quartzofeldspathic
gneiss samples have well-deﬁned secondary magnetizations of
low coercivity and laboratory unblocking temperatures that are
readily removed during demagnetization ( Fig. 7 B). The sec-
ondary magnetization is of north declination and moderate
positive inclination with a site-mean direction of D = 2.5
◦ and
I = 76.6◦ (k = 504.6, α95 = 2.5◦ n = 8 samples). Because of its
ready removal during demagnetization and its normal polar-
ity direction, this magnetization is probably a VRM acquired
in the present-day or Recent geomagnetic ﬁelds. With fur-
ther demagnetization, these samples give a magnetization of
north to northeast declination and moderate to steep negative
inclination. A site-mean direction from this component gives
D = 34.8
◦ and I = −61.7◦ (k = 51.7, α95 = 7.2◦, n = 8 samples),
which is essentially identical to the remanence of the dike
(Fig. 7 A and Fig. 8 A). The similarity of directions between
the dike and host gneiss samples strongly suggests that the
dike has baked the adjacent gneiss to form a TRM and that
the dike magnetization is primary and was acquired during
cooling following dike emplacement. AF and thermal demagne-
tization characteristics, particularly the complete unblocking of
the magnetization at temperatures below 580
◦C, indicate that
the magnetization in the baked contact samples is carried by
magnetite.

conﬁdence level, suggesting that the baked contact test is negative. However, 40Ar/39Ar dating of biotite from one of the host samples yields an apparent age of
787 Ma, which is consistent with the apparent age of the dikes as determined by U–Pb and 40Ar/39Ar dates on hornblende from the group B dikes. We suggest that
the apparent discordance of the dike and gneiss directions may be due to deﬂection of the magnetic vector by the strong metamorphic fabric of the gneiss samples.
The similarity of directions and the concordance of the biotite 40Ar/39Ar date from these samples suggests that the baked contact test should be considered to be
positive and that the B1 magnetization is a thermoremanent magnetization acquired during cooling following emplacement of the group B dikes.
The second baked contact test is from a 5-m wide dike, which
has a characteristic direction of southwest declination and steep
positive inclination. At this locality, we collected 12 samples
along a traverse perpendicular to the dike contact out for 8 m.
Gneiss samples from within a meter of the dike yield magnetiza-
tions that are essentially identical to that of the dike (Fig. 9A–C).
Five samples collected within a meter of the dike give a mean
direction of D = 248.9
◦, I = 60.0◦ (k = 40.4, α95 = 12.2◦), which
is essentially identical to the dike mean direction ofD = 257.1◦,
I = 64.5◦ (k = 43.5, α95 = 4.8◦, n = 22 samples; dike 6, Table 2)
(Fig. 8B). At greater distances from the contact, magnetizations
in the gneiss are either randomly oriented, directionally unsta-
ble, or of low coercivity and similar to the present-day ﬁeld
direction ( Fig. 9 D). The baked contact results from this site
strongly suggest gneiss magnetization was caused by thermal
affects accompanying dike emplacement. Rock magnetic char-
acteristics indicate that magnetizations in baked and unbaked
gneiss samples are carried by magnetite.

The presence of antipodal baked contact tests strongly sug-
gests that the magnetization in both contact zones was caused
by thermal affects associated with dike emplacement and that
the observed dike normal and reverse polarity magnetizations
are primary TRMs. Unfortunately, although these tests suggest
a primary origin for the A
1 remanence, they are not fully conclu-
sive because we cannot demonstrate that the dike magnetizations
are superimposed on geologically stable, preexisting magneti-
zations in the gneiss. However, we note that the gneiss samples
well removed from the thermal effects of the Proterozoic dikes
typically do not yield coherent magnetizations of any geologic
age (Fig. 9E).

### page_17
S.S. Harlan et al. / Precambrian Research 163 (2008) 239–264 255
4.2. B 1 Magnetization
Ninety-one percent of samples from group B dikes gave inter-
pretable and usable paleomagnetic results. NRM directions are
dominated by magnetizations of north declination and moder-
ate positive inclination, although there is signiﬁcant streaking
towards northwest declinations and shallow inclinations. The
range of NRM intensities (8.2× 10
−5 to 14.8× 101 A/m) is sim-
ilar to that of the dikes with the A1 magnetization, but the mean
is signiﬁcantly lower (i.e. 7.97× 10−1 A/m). Following demag-
netization, paleomagnetic samples from the group B dikes gave
results that can be divided into two types: (1) samples in which
a well-deﬁned, univectorial magnetization of northwest decli-
nation and shallow negative inclination, the B
1 remanence, is
readily isolated (40% of samples); (2) those in which the B 1
magnetization is partially to almost completely dominated by
secondary magnetizations such that the characteristic direction
could not be fully isolated (43.6% of samples); and (3) those
that are completely dominated by a magnetization of north dec-
lination and moderate inclination, termed the R magnetization,
discussed in a subsequent section (7.5% of samples).
Samples in which the B
1 remanence is well deﬁned are typ-
ically from ﬁne-grained (<1 mm diameter) phases or chilled
zones of the group B dikes. Secondary overprints, where present,
are minor and easily removed by AF or thermal demagnetization
(Fig. 10A and B). The B
1 remanence in these samples is char-
acterized by moderate to high MDFs (30–70 mT). Normalized
intensity decay curves from thermally demagnetized samples are
usually “knee-shaped” indicating a discrete range of laboratory
unblocking temperatures with 60–80% of the NRM unblocked
between 520 and 580
◦C. IRM acquisition experiments and AF
demagnetization of NRM and IRM behavior and hysteresis data
(Fig. 6B and D) suggest that this magnetization is carried by a
combination of single- and/or pseudosingle domain magnetite.
Strong-ﬁeld thermomagnetic curves are reversible and give a
single Curie point at 565 ± 10
◦C( n = 3 samples), indicative of
low-Ti titanomagnetite (Fig. 6F). Stable endpoints obtained from
these samples are well grouped about a northwest, moderate neg-
ative inclination direction. We consider this direction to be the
ChRM of the group B dikes.
Isolation of the B
1 magnetization in other group B dike sam-
ples was somewhat problematic. Most samples are dominated
Fig. 10. (A and B) Orthogonal vector diagrams and equal-area projections showing the behavior of paleomagnetic samples from group B dikes that yield well-deﬁned
univectorial decay of the B1 magnetization vector during thermal and AF demagnetization. (C) Vector diagram and equal-area projection of a sample from a group B
dike in which the characteristic remanent magnetization could not be isolated due to the overlap of coercivity and unblocking temperature spectra with a magnetization
of north declination and moderate positive inclination. For most samples which displayed such behavior, the characteristic remanent magnetizatio n could not be
isolated in AF or thermal demagnetization as the remanence became erratic at high AF ﬁelds or temperatures. For such samples, remagnetization circleanalysis was
applied as described in the text. Conventions as in Fig. 4.

### page_18
256 S.S. Harlan et al. / Precambrian Research 163 (2008) 239–264
by well-deﬁned secondary magnetizations of north declination
and moderate positive inclination ( Fig. 10C). This overprint is
characterized by low to moderate coercivities and distributed
laboratory unblocking temperatures. Up to 60% of the NRM is
usually removed by 15–20 mT, or by 250–300
◦C. A mode based
on 157 overprint directions is D = 356.6◦, I = 64.1◦ (β95 = 3.1◦),
which is similar to both latest Cretaceous/early Tertiary magne-
tizations and the time-averaged and present-day ﬁeld directions
for the site area. It is possible that the observed magnetization is a
VRM of recent origin, but partial remagnetization by Cretceous
or Tertiary thermal events cannot be ruled out. At higher
demagnetization levels, the secondary magnetization is grad-
ually removed, with the resultant remanence directions deﬁning
a great circle path toward the B
1 direction deﬁned by the stable
endpoints described above. Due to the overlap of the coercivity
and unblocking temperature spectra of these magnetizations, and
the common onset of erratic directional and intensity changes
at peak ﬁelds greater than 60 mT, the ChRM of many of these
samples is rarely fully isolated. The erratic behavior is proba-
bly caused by the acquisition of a spurious, laboratory induced
anhysteretic remanent magnetization during AF demagnetiza-
tion. Most samples that show this behavior are from coarse-
grained, dike interiors and contain large (up to 0.5–1.0 mm)
titanomagnetite-ilmenite grains. Thermal and low temperature
demagnetization methods were similarly ineffective in isolating
the ChRM of many samples. Most thermally demagnetized sam-
ples became unstable at temperatures above 350
◦C. Sulﬁde min-
erals are common in these rocks, and this behavior may reﬂect
their thermal breakdown to create new magnetic phases during
the demagnetization experiments. Most data used in the calcu-
lation of site-mean directions from these rocks are based on AF
results.
Paleomagnetic and rock magnetic characteristics of the
coarse-grained group B dikes indicate that their magnetization
is carried by a combination of multidomain and single-domain
or pseudosingle-domain magnetite. AF demagnetization curves
show rapid decay of NRM at low ﬁelds, followed by grad-
ual decay of the NRM at higher ﬁelds. Saturation of IRM
occurs in ﬁelds of less than 150 mT, and the saturation IRM is
usually more resistant to AF demagnetization than the NRM
(Fig. 6 E). This behavior is typical of samples in which the
remanence is dominated by multidomain magnetite, and this
phase likely carries the pronounced VRM in these samples. The
streaked distribution toward northwest declinations and shallow
inclinations may be due to the presence of small amounts of
ﬁne-grained, single domain or pseudosingle domain magnetite
which carries the B
1 magnetization. The magnetite probably
occurs as ﬁne inclusions in plagioclase and/or ferromagne-
sian minerals. Two thermomagnetic curves from magnetic
extracts showed reversible behavior and Curie temperatures
of 560 and 565
◦C indicating they are low-Ti titanomag-
netite.
Estimating the grand-mean direction for the group B dikes
is difﬁcult owing to the large number of samples that did
not yield stable endpoints. Given the large number of sam-
ples that only yielded great circles, most site-mean directions
were calculated by calculating remagnetization circles and com-
bining these with stable endpoints to yield estimates of the
site-mean directions (McFadden and McElhinny, 1988). Remag-
netization circles used in the analysis were well determined,
as evidenced by MAD values which ranged from 1.5
◦ to 12◦,
with 90% less than 5 ◦. Most sites have at least some sam-
ples that yielded stable endpoints, and site-mean directions
determined by this method yielded well-deﬁned means of north-
west declination and shallow negative inclination. Individual
site means yielded k values ranging from 15 to 206, with
α
95 values of 4.5 ◦ to 23.0◦ (Fig. 5 C; Table 2). The 23 indi-
vidual sites from the group B dikes are combined to yield
what we interpret to be 12 independent readings of the geo-
magnetic ﬁeld, with a grand-mean direction of D = 301.5
◦,
I = −17.1◦ (k = 117, α95 = 4.0◦)( Fig. 5 D, Table 3 ), which
we consider to be the best estimate of the B 1 magnetiza-
tion.
To assess whether, the B 1 magnetization is primary, ﬁve
samples from host gneiss from one locality were collected for
a baked contact test. All samples were collected within dis-
tance of 0.2 m from a 35-m wide group B dike (Fig. 8C) which
has a characteristic dike-mean magnetization of D = 296.6
◦ and
I = −11.9◦ (k = 142, α95 = 6.4◦, N = 6 sites; dike 16, Table 2).
These samples were used for isotopic dating, and thus were
only demagnetized by AF methods. The gneiss samples contain
two magnetization components. The ﬁrst is of low coerciv-
ity and gives a direction of north declination and moderate
positive inclination; it is probably a VRM acquired in the
present-day ﬁeld. The second component yields characteristic
directions of west declination and shallow negative inclination
(Fig. 11A and B), with a site-mean ofD = 269.1
◦ and I = −23.2◦
(k = 116.5, α95 = 7.1◦, n = 5 samples) (Fig. 8D). Although sim-
ilar in inclination to that observed from the adjacent dike, the
dike and contact zone site-mean directions are distinct at the
95% conﬁdence level ( Fig. 8D). This result suggests that the
two magnetizations are different and that the baked contact
test is negative, which is surprising given the proximity of the
gneiss samples to the dike contact and the thickness of the
dike. Biotite separated from one of the paleomagnetic baked
contact samples in the gneiss at site TR50 gives an apparent
age similar to the age of dike emplacement obtained by U–Pb
and
40Ar/39Ar systems (discussed below) indicating that the
gneiss sample was heated to temperatures during dike intru-
sion sufﬁcient to reset its biotite
40Ar/39Ar system. Because
of the strongly anisotropic fabric of the host gneiss, the dis-
cordance of the dike and gneiss site-mean directions may be
due to deﬂection of the remanence vector by the metamorphic
rock fabric. The rock magnetic fabric was not measured prior
to destruction of the rock samples for mineral separations for
dating purposes, so this hypothesis could not be tested. The
results of the paleomagnetic baked contact test alone cannot
be used to establish whether the observed B dike magnetization
is a primary TRM or is due to a younger remagnetization, but
the concordance of the
40Ar/39Ar age spectra with hornblendes
from the dike and the biotite from the host gneiss sample at
this site indicate that the argon systems of these rocks have not
been signiﬁcantly thermally reset since dike emplacement at ca.
780 Ma.

4.3. R magnetization
The R magnetization is characterized by well-deﬁned, uni-
vectorial magnetizations of north to northwest declination and
moderate to steep inclination ( Fig. 12 A and B). In general,
this magnetization is mostly restricted to group B dikes, or is
found in dikes of uncertain afﬁliation such as in sites TR55
and 56, from the Mammoth dike in the northern Tobacco Root
Mountains ( Fig. 2 b). Samples that contain the R magnetiza-
tion are characterized by moderate to high MDFs (25–60 mT),
distributed laboratory unblocking temperatures below 580
◦C,
and 95–98% saturation of IRM by 300 mT. These observa-
tions indicate that the magnetization is dominated by a low
coercivity phase, such as magnetite. A single thermomagnetic
analysis of a magnetic extract from a Mammoth dike sam-
ple (not shown) gave reversible heating and cooling curves
with a Curie temperature of 575
◦C, which indicates that the
extract is nearly pure magnetite. Petrographic observations
indicate that magnetite and ilmenite, as oxidation-exsolution
products of titanomagnetite, are common in these rocks. The
paleomagnetic and rock magnetic evidence indicates that the
R magnetization in these samples is carried by low-Ti mag-
netite.
The northwest declination and positive inclination direc-
tion for the R magnetization suggests that is of secondary
origin and signiﬁcantly younger than the A
1 or B 1 magneti-
zations, which we consider primary TRMs. However, its origin
is not clear for all samples. In some cases, such as in group
B sites that show partial to complete recovery of the B
1 rema-
nence, the R magnetization may result from failure to remove
the pronounced VRM present in these samples. This appears
unlikely, given that most samples with this magnetization have
declinations that are signiﬁcantly west of the present-day or
time-averaged ﬁeld directions. In other cases, the R magne-
tization is associated with highly altered or heavily fractured
parts of dikes. At site TR20, for example, the R magnetiza-
tion is in samples from the intensely epidotized dike margin
of a group B dike, whereas it is only found in one sam-
ple from the fresh dike interior. Similarly, paleomagnetic sites
TR55 and TR56 are in a dike pervasively fractured due to
Laramide thrust movement along the adjacent Mammoth fault.
For such sites, we suspect that the R magnetization reﬂects
complete remagnetization by Late Cretaceous or early Tertiary
hydrothermal ﬂuids, resulting in a magnetization carried by mag-
netite.
The NRM directions of the small Laramide pluton are south
directed and have steep to moderate negative inclinations, with
NRM intensities between 1.55 × 10
−1 and 3.03 × 10−1 A/m.
AF demagnetization is characterized by moderate to high
median destructive ﬁelds (50–60 mT) and univectorial decay
of the magnetic vector ( Fig. 12 C). Thermal demagnetiza-
tion showed unblocking temperatures that ranged from 250
to >620
◦C, indicating that this magnetization is carried by
a combination of magnetite and hematite. The mean direc-
tion is D = 191.0
◦, I = −68.1◦ (k = 110, α95 = 5.8◦)( Fig. 13 ;
Table 2).
Fig. 13. In situ equal-area projection showing mean directions and α95 cones
of conﬁdence for dikes that contain the R magnetization. The R magnetization
is considered to be a Late Cretaceous or early Tertiary magnetization that has
completely overprinted the remanence in some dike samples. The group-mean
direction for the R magnetization is shown by the star. Also shown is the site
mean direction (square) for a northwest-striking Proterozoic maﬁc dike in the
Madison Range that was remagnetized during Late Cretaceous/early Tertiary
time. The upward-pointing triangle shows the site-mean from a Late Cretaceous
intrusion exposed in the southern Tobacco Root Mountains; the downward-
pointing triangles are paleomagnetic sites from the Tobacco Root Batholith
reported by Hanna (1973) ; the site-mean shown by the arrow was not used
in calculating a summary Late Cretceous/early Tertiary direction as described
in the text because of its large α
95.
5. Discussion
Proterozoic maﬁc dikes in the Tobacco Root of southwest
Montana yield three remanent magnetizations. The A 1 and
B1 magnetizations are distinctly different from each other and
both are unlike magnetizations associated with any part of the
Phanerozoic APW path for North America. As discussed below,
we consider them to be primary magnetizations of Proterozoic
age. TheR magnetization is probably of Late Cretaceous or early
Tertiary age. To compare the magnetizations from these rocks
with reference poles derived from elsewhere in North America,
we converted site-mean directions to a common polarity and cal-
culated virtual geomagnetic poles (VGPs) for the three groups,
assuming an axially geocentric dipole ﬁeld.
The A
1 magnetization is found in Wooden et al.’s (1978)
geochemical group A dikes and one group C dike (i.e., dike
9, Table 2). The remanence is well deﬁned by dual polarity
magnetizations and there is no apparent difference between the
paleomagnetic data obtained from the Group A and Group C
dikes. Although not antipodal, we consider the best estimate of
the A
1 direction to include both the normal and reverse polar-
ity data sets and this yields an in situ grand-mean direction of
D = 225.0
◦, I = 61.8◦ (k = 27.9, α95 = 7.7◦, N = 14 independent
readings of the geomagnetic ﬁeld). Averaging the VGPs gives
a paleomagnetic pole located in the central Paciﬁc Ocean at

S.S. Harlan et al. / Precambrian Research 163 (2008) 239–264 259

poles from the Mesoproterozoic Belt Supergroup, open circles are Meso- and Neoproterozoic poles, downward-pointing triangles are poles from sedimentary strata
of the Uinta Mountains and Grand Canyon, upward-pointing triangles are poles from ca. 780 Ma intrusions of the Gunbarrel magmatic event, diamonds are poles
from the 723 Ma Franklin Dikes. Also shown are 95% conﬁdence limits for selected poles. TRA = mean pole for the Tobacco Root Mountains A 1 magnetization

CI = Croker Island; LAC/SG = Laramie anorthosite complex/Sherman Granite; SF = St. Francois Mountains V olcanics; ELG = Electra Lake Gabbro; BSm = meanof
Belt Supergroup Poles; TRB = mean pole for the Tobacco Root Mountains B1 magnetization; H = Hottah maﬁc sheets; S = McKenzie dikes; B = Christmas Lake dike

and Jefferson (1991), Park et al. (1995a), Weil et al. (2003), Weil et al. (1998, 2004, 2006), and Warnock et al., 2000).
216.1◦E, 8.7◦N( K = 15.8, A95 = 10.3◦)( Table 3). Remanence
acquisition in the A1 dikes spanned at least two polarity chrons,
or a minimum of several tens of thousands of years indicat-
ing that the A
1 magnetization has averaged some paleosecular
variation (PSV). The fact that the normal and reverse polarity
directions are not antipodal may indicate that PSV has not been
fully averaged or that the age of emplacement of the normal
and reverse polarity dikes and dikes of group A and C resulted
from discrete but temporally restricted magmatic events dur-
ing the Mesoproterozoic. However, the precision of available
geochronology does not allow such a difference in age to be
distinguished.
The presence of essentially identical magnetizations in dikes
of geochemical groups A and C, which provided Rb–Sr dates
of 1455 and 1100 Ma, respectively, suggests that the geologic
reliability of at least one of the Rb–Sr dates is questionable given
the similarity in paleomagnetic directions from the group A and
C dikes. Comparison of the combined group A and C poles,
which plot at near equatorial latitudes and ca. 1100 Ma poles
that plot at signiﬁcantly higher north latitudes and more west-
ern longitudes ( Fig. 14) indicate that the 1100 Ma Rb–Sr date
is not supported by the paleomagnetic results from this study.
Sm–Nd dating of minerals from a paleomagnetic core sample of
a reverse polarity Group A dike yields an age of 1448 ± 49 Ma
(Harlan et al., 2005). This age conﬁrms the validity of the group
A Rb–Sr age of Wooden et al. (1978), but is more precise. This
age is considered to be the best estimate for the emplacement
age of the group A dikes. The similarity between paleomagnetic
directions between the group A and C dikes suggests that they
were probably emplaced at about the same time. Furthermore,
as discussed below, the paleomagnetic poles from the group A
and C dikes are similar to poles from ca. 1450 Ma rocks else-
where in North America (e.g. Harlan and Geissman, 1998) and
are signiﬁcantly different from poles of ca. 1100 Ma. Thus, we
suggest that the 1100 Ma Rb–Sr date reported for the group C
dikes is not reliable.
Assuming that the A
1 magnetization is a primary TRM and
that the Wyoming and Laurentian cratons were joined by Meso-
proterozoic time ( Hoffman, 1988; Dutch and Nielsen, 1990;
Mueller and Frost, 2006; Foster et al., 2006 ), we compare the
A
1 paleomagnetic pole with poles from rocks of similar age
elsewhere in North America ( Fig. 14 ). The in situ A 1 pole
plots slightly north of the main locus of poles from ca. 1450
to 1420 Ma intrusions from Labrador, the central U.S., and the
Rocky Mountains. The apparent agreement between the A
1 pole
and the other 1450–1420 Ma poles is remarkable given that the
A
1 pole has not been corrected for potential post-emplacement
tilting.

### page_22
260 S.S. Harlan et al. / Precambrian Research 163 (2008) 239–264
The group B dikes give an in situ grand-mean direction of
D = 301.5◦, I = −17.1◦, k = 117, α95 = 4.0◦, N = 12 independent
readings), with a paleomagnetic pole in the western Paciﬁc
Ocean at 14.6
◦N, 127.0◦E, (K = 190, A95 = 3.2◦)( Table 3), north
of present-day New Guinea ( Fig. 14 ). U–Pb and 40Ar/39Ar
geochronologic data from group B dikes reported in Harlan et
al. (2005) and this study was obtained from hand samples col-
lected from the same rocks sampled at paleomagnetic sites TR6,
TR19, TR21, TR62, and TR50; these data indicate that these
dikes were intruded at 780 Ma. Furthermore, the VGP from the
group B dikes is concordant with VGPs from Neoproterozoic
maﬁc intrusions elsewhere in western North America, including
the northwest-striking Christmas Lake and Mount Moran dikes
in the nearby Beartooth and Teton Ranges, respectively (Harlan
et al., 1997 ), the Hottah sheets of the northwestern Canadian
Shield (Park et al., 1995a ) and maﬁc dikes in the Mackenzie
Mountains of the Northwest Territories ( Park, 1981; Park et
al., 1989)( Fig. 14). Several of these rocks (the Hottah sheets,
Mackenzie dikes, and the Christmas Lake dike) give isotopic
dates of ca. 780 Ma by either the U–Pb or
40Ar/39Ar methods
(Heaman et al., 1991; LeCheminant and Heaman, 1994; Park
et al., 1995b; Harlan et al., 2003b ). The VGP is also similar to
the normal and reverse polarity poles from the 723 Ma Franklin
dikes of northern Canada ( Park and Jefferson, 1991; Heaman
et al., 1991 )( Fig. 14 ) and some sedimentary rocks from the
Uinta Mountains Supergroup and the Galeros Formation of the
Chuar Group of the Grand Canyon Supergroup (Weil et al., 2004,
2006).
The concordance of both the group A
1 and B1 poles with
those from rocks of similar age is striking and implies that the
basement rocks into which they intrude have not been signif-
icantly tilted since emplacement of the dikes at ca. 1450 and
780 Ma. However, small-magnitude post-emplacement tilting
cannot be unequivocally ruled out because of the angular discor-
dance that does exist between the Tobacco Root group A
1 dike
pole and those from the Belt Supergroup that plot signiﬁcantly
to the south (Fig. 14). The rocks from which the Belt poles are
derived were emplaced between 1470 and 1400 Ma ( Evans et
al., 2000), with the poles from the Belt Supergroup interpreted
to represent a stillstand in the North American APW during this
time (Elston et al., 2002). Numerous workers, as early as the late
1970’s (e.g.Irving, 1979), have noted that Belt Supergroup poles
plot signiﬁcantly south of most ca. 1400 Ma poles from else-
where in North America, which are mostly from intrusive rocks
that lack a record of paleohorizontal. At least some of this discor-
dance between poles derived from these igneous rocks broadly
distributed across Laurentia and those of the Belt Supergroup
could be the result of post-emplacement tilting of the intrusive
rocks, as well as failure of some of the poles from intrusive
rocks, such as the Tobacco Root dikes, to fully average pale-
osecular variation. Nonetheless, neither of these explanations
adequately explain why most poles from intrusions are discor-
dant with those of the Belt Supergroup. An additional possibility
is that the areas where most of the Belt Supergroup data have
been obtained have experienced some degree of vertical axis
rotation since remanence acquisition, as explored by Elston et
al. (2002). Furthermore, despite magnetic and ﬁeld-based tests
(e.g. reversal and fold tests) of the antiquity of the remanence
in the Belt Supergroup rocks, it remains possible that the rocks
were remagnetized over along period of time prior to deforma-
tion and that workers have been comparing magnetizations of
substantially different age. Another possibility, consistent with
the relative distribution of the poles is that the Belt Supergroup
poles have been systematically affected by inclination shallow-
ing. At present the discordance between the poles from the ca.
1470 and 1400 Ma sedimentary rocks of the Belt Supergroup
and intrusive rocks from Laurentia remains poorly understood.
The extent to which post-emplacement tilting may affect
the remanence in intrusions, such as those in this study, is a
problem that is endemic to the use of plutonic rocks to deter-
mine paleomagnetic poles for tectonic studies. To assess whether
post-emplacement tilting may have affected the magnetizations
characteristic of group A and B dikes, we compare the pale-
omagnetic direction from the secondary R magnetization with
expected directions from reference directions for North Amer-
ica, and compare our observed primary poles with those of
equivalent age from elsewhere in North America. These compar-
isons suggest that post-dike emplacement tilting of the Tobacco
Root has been minimal.
The overall mean of the R magnetization, which we inter-
pret to be a Late Cretaceous/early Tertiary magnetization, as
well as two sites in Late Cretaceous intrusions, after inver-
sion to normal polarity, yield a combined mean of D = 346.8
◦,
I = 64.2◦ (k = 46.6, α95 = 8.2◦; Fig. 13 , Table 3 ). The origin
of this secondary magnetization is not known with certainty,
but we consider it to likely have resulted from remagnetiza-
tion by hydrothermal ﬂuids associated with Late Cretaceous
or Tertiary thermal activity. Evidence for such a remagnetiza-
tion is compelling along the Mammoth fault in the northern
Tobacco Root Mountains where a Laramide thrust fault intensely
sheared and fractured the Mammoth diabase dike (Fig. 2B). The
fault controlled the emplacement of the Tobacco Root Batholith
(Schmidt et al., 1990 ) and acted as a conduit for late stage
magmatic ﬂuids or ﬂuids associated with subsequent precious
mineralization. Evidence for ﬂuid activity includes extensive
chloritization and epidotization of the dike, and locally intense
siliciﬁcation. The remanence may have been caused by growth
of secondary magnetite around original titanomagnetite grains,
by growth of new magnetite by precipitation of iron during for-
mation of secondary alteration phases, or by a combination of
both processes. Some magnetite may also have formed during
oxidation of magmatic sulﬁdes present within the dike. It is
unlikely to be the result of widespread tectonothermal activity
with temperatures greater than 300
◦C given the preservation
of Proterozoic ages from biotites in basement rocks from the
southern Tobacco Root Mountains, including the biotite from
the baked contact zone at site TR50 described above. A similar
relationship between intense shearing and fracturing of maﬁc
dikes near or along Laramide faults, hydrothermal ﬂuids, and a
magnetite-dominated remagnetization of Proterozoic dikes has
been observed in the nearby Highland Mountains and Madison
Range (Harlan et al., 1996; Harlan, unpublished data). The age
of this secondary magnetization may be closely approximated
by the 7 Ma age of the Tobacco Root Batholith ( Vitaliano et

### page_23
S.S. Harlan et al. / Precambrian Research 163 (2008) 239–264 261
al., 1980). Alternatively, it may be somewhat younger as sug-
gested by 40Ar/39Ar dates of 67–66 Ma from sericite formed
during potassic alteration by hydrothermal ﬂuids in the Pony
Mining district located in the northeastern part of the Tobacco
Root Mountains (Myers and Snee, unpublished data). The R
magnetization of dikes in the southern Tobacco Root Mountains
probably originated in a similar manner, but complete remagne-
tization appears to have been limited to some samples from dike
margins or from zones of pervasive Laramide fractures that cut
the basement rocks and diabase dikes. Most dikes in the south-
ern Tobacco Root Mountains are not found near major Laramide
faults or shear zones and thus escaped extensive remagnetiza-
tion.
Comparison of theR and Late Cretaceous/early Tertiary mag-
netization (Table 3) with the expected 75 Ma reference direction
(D = 352.6
◦, I = 66.7◦, α95 = 3.1◦) for the study area based on
the pole from the Adel Mountain V olcanics of western Montana
(Gunderson and Sheriff, 1991 ) yields a statistically indistin-
guishable difference of 2.6± 6.4
◦ using the method of Debiche
and Watson (1995). Assuming that the R magnetization is Late
Cretaceous or early Tertiary in age, any appreciable tilting of the
basement rocks must have occurred prior to this time. Further-
more, the presence of ﬂat-lying 53–33 Ma volcanic rocks north
of Virginia City (Marvin et al., 1974) indicate that post-middle
Tertiary tilting, possibly associated with late Cenozoic extension
is minimal.
Because emplacement of the Late Cretaceous Tobacco Root
Batholith was synchronous with displacement along northwest-
striking, Laramide-age basement-involved faults in the Tobacco
Root Mountains (Schmidt et al., 1990), it is possible that at least
some tilting of the range may have occurred prior to intrusion of
the batholith. Overall, the Tobacco Root Mountains have been
proposed to be tilted to the east or northeast, although a spe-
ciﬁc magnitude for tilting has not been quantiﬁed (Burger et al.,
2004; Harms et al., 2004). To investigate the effects of possible
northeast-tilt of the basement rocks on the paleomagnetic data
reported here we have corrected the paleomagnetic poles for
tilt about a northwest-striking axis of N50
◦W, the overall strike
of major faults that cut the core of the range. We correct the
poles from the group A and B dikes for 10
◦ and 20◦ northeast-
side-down tilt to show how this would affect their position with
respect to age-equivalent poles. Greater magnitude of tilt is not
justiﬁed given that the Proterozoic dikes in the Tobacco Root
Mountains are near vertical. Application of this tilt correction
increases the discordance between the mean pole from the group
A dikes and poles from the ca. 1450 Ma intrusions and Belt
Supergroup rocks ( Fig. 14). In contrast, the model tilt correc-
tion has little or no affect on the pole from the group B dikes
(tilt correction results not shown) because the strike of the tilt
axis is sub-parallel to that of the B
1 declination and the mean
inclination is shallow. For example, correcting the pole from the
group B dikes for 10
◦ and 20◦ tilts results in an angular differ-
ence between the in situ and tilt corrected poles of 1.9 ± 3.4◦
and 4.8 ± 3.4◦, respectively.
The discrepancy between the Tobacco Root group A 1 pole
and those from the Belt Supergroup is problematic because the
dikes and the sedimentary rocks are identical in age, although the
age of remanence in the Belt Supergroup rocks remains open to
question. Furthermore, the group A dikes are considered to have
been emplaced during extension accompanying development of
the Belt Basin. Comparison of the group A
1 pole with the mean
Belt Supergroup pole ( Fig. 14) yields an angular discordance
of 29.1 ± 8.1◦. Assuming that the group A dikes adequately
averaged paleosecular variation and that the Belt Supergroup
remanence is of equivalent age, this discordance would require
a tilt correction of 58
◦ (west-side-down) about a strike of N6◦E
to bring the group A dike pole into coincidence with poles of
the Belt Supergroup. Unless this tilting occurred prior to the
emplacement of the younger group B dikes, this would displace
the group B pole to 57.0
◦N, 162.3◦E, making it signiﬁcantly dis-
cordant with respect to poles from the other 780 Ma intrusions
(e.g. Gunbarrel poles). There appears to be no evidence that a
west-side-down tilt of such magnitude affected the basement
rocks of southwestern Montana.
Overall, the general agreement between the ca. 1450 Ma pole
from the group A dikes with other ca. 1450 Ma intrusions, as well
as the excellent agreement between the pole from the group B
dikes with those from other 780 Ma dikes ( Fig. 14), indicates
that the basement rocks of the Tobacco Root Mountains have
not experienced signiﬁcant tilting or vertical-axis rotation since
emplacement of the dikes in the Meso- and Neoproterozoic time.
Although some of the discordance between the pole from the
group A and C dikes and those of the Belt Supergroup could
reﬂect incomplete averaging of paleosecular variation, the over-
all disagreement between ca. 1.45 to 1.4 Ga poles derived from
most igneous rocks from North America and those from the Belt
Supergroup continues to be problematic.
6. Conclusions
Proterozoic maﬁc dikes from the southern Tobacco Root
Mountains contain three distinct magnetizations that provide
insight and improved understanding of the geologic, magmatic,
and tectonic evolution of southwestern Montana and the west-
ern Cordillera. In addition, they provide key paleomagnetic poles
that contribute to increased resolution of the Meso- and Neopro-
terozoic parts of the North American APW path.
Paleomagnetic directions from geochemically deﬁned group
A and C dikes yield similar magnetizations indicating that rema-
nence acquisition in both groups occurred at about the same time.
Concordant Rb–Sr and Sm–Nd dates of 1455 and 1448 Ma indi-
cate that the dikes were emplaced during the Mesoproterozoic;
baked contact tests indicate that the observed remanent mag-
netization is a thermoremanent magnetization acquired during
dike emplacement. A mean paleomagnetic pole from the group
A dikes is consistent with those of most ca. 1450 Ma intrusions
from elsewhere in North America, but is discordant with age
equivalent strata of the nearby Belt Basin. The reason for this
discordance is unknown, but is not due to signiﬁcant tilting of
the basement rocks of the Tobacco Root Mountains.
Paleomagnetic results from group B dikes yield a magnetiza-
tion that is considered to be primary. U–Pb baddeleyite analyses
indicate that the dikes were emplaced at 782 Ma, and hornblende
40Ar/39Ar dates from the group B dikes are consistent with this

### page_24
262 S.S. Harlan et al. / Precambrian Research 163 (2008) 239–264
age. Biotite from a contact zone from one of the dikes yields
a reset 40Ar/39Ar date of 788 Ma. Together, these data indi-
cate that most of dikes have not been signiﬁcantly thermally
disturbed since emplacement in the Neoproterozoic. Overall,
the isotopic dates from the Tobacco Root Mountains document
two distinct episodes of emplacement of subparallel northwest-
striking maﬁc dikes, separated by an interval of ∼700 Ma. The
paleomagnetic pole from the group B dikes is consistent with
those obtained from other 780 to 770 Ma intrusions elsewhere
in the western Cordillera. As noted by Park et al. (1995b), this
consistency demonstrates the tectonic integrity of the western
Cordillera and indicates that little or no relative rotation has
occurred between these regions since 780 Ma. Together, these
ca. 780 Ma dikes are part of regional magmatic episode termed
the Gunbarrel Maﬁc Magmatic Event that may have been a pre-
cursor to crustal extension and rifting that resulted in the break
up of Rodinia and development of the proto-Paciﬁc Ocean (Park
et al., 1995b; Harlan et al., 2003b, 2005 ). A combined and
revised paleomagnetic pole utilizing data from this study and
other 780 Ma Gunbarrel dikes and sills (Park, 1981; Park et al.,
1989; Park et al., 1995a ; Harlan et al., 1997 ) yields a pole at
9.2
◦N, 138.7◦E( K = 72.6, A95 = 9.0◦, N = 6 VGPs) and provides
a key reference pole for Neoproterozoic plate reconstructions,
especially if matching dike segments of identical age can be
found on now widely dispersed continental fragments.
Although primary magnetizations were recovered from most
Proterozoic dikes sampled during this study, some dikes showed
evidence of partial to complete remagnetization yielding well-
deﬁned magnetizations identical to those expected from latest
Cretaceous to early Tertiary time. The origin of this magneti-
zation is not clear, but in some cases is thought to be due to
heavy fracturing of dikes adjacent to Laramide-age fault zones
and hydrothermal ﬂuid ﬂow causing growth of new magnetite.
Remagnetization due to hydrothermal activity due to Laramide
intrusive activity and faulting has been proposed to account for
apparent Late Cretaceous remagnetization of Proterozoic dikes
elsewhere in Montana. A combined mean direction from the
dikes that contain the Late Cretceous remagnetization and pale-
omagnetic data from Late Cretaceous intrusions associated with
the Tobacco Root Batholith yield a mean direction identical to
that for the expected 75 Ma reference direction for the study
area. The combination of data for all age rocks indicates that
the Tobacco Root Mountains have not experienced signiﬁcant
tilting or vertical-axis rotation since emplacement in Meso- and
Neoproterozoic time.
